title: Liber Adversus Origenem
author: Justinianus Imperator

statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Ac necesse erit omnino dicere, ipsum Deum opificem hominis, corpus esse, ut pote qui corpus ad imaginem et similitudinem suam fecerit. Quomodo autem corpus, imago incorporei esse possit ? Quamobrem absit, ut his Christiani assentian- tur. Si vero, juxta Origenis blasphemiam, animæ præexistebant, ac in poenam peccatorum suorum in corpora demissæ sunt, ut emendatæ resipiscerent, eas oportebat amplius non peccare. Nam si corpus datum est animæ in supplicium propter peccata, ut doloribus emendaretur ad honorificandum Deum, quomodo corpus cam adjuvat et corroborat ad peccandum, quod iis qui poena afficiuntur, non evenit ?
passages.english: And it will be wholly necessary to say that God himself, the maker of man, is a body, inasmuch as he made a body in his own image and likeness. But how could a body be the image of the incorporeal? Therefore far be it that Christians should assent to these things. But if, according to the blasphemy of Origen, souls pre-existed and were sent down into bodies as a punishment for their sins, so that, once corrected, they might come to their senses, they ought to sin no more. For if the body was given to the soul as a punishment on account of sins, so that it might be corrected by pains to honour God, how does the body help and strengthen it to sin, which does not happen to those who are subjected to punishment?

passages.original: Quoniam autem Origenes ad coeteras blasphemias hoc adjunxit, Domini animam prius exstilisse, eique Deum Verbum esse unitum antequam e Virgine incarnaretur : hoc etiam deliramentum evertens ipse sanctus Athanasius in epistola ad Epictetum, sic dicit : < Merito sese damnabunt omnes qui existimant ante Mariam esse carnem, quae ex ea est; ac ante eam habuisse animam humanam Deum Verbum, ac iu ea ante adventum semper fuisse. > Quare si ex iis quæ a sancto Alhanasio dicta sunt, anima Domini nostri Jesu Chrisli, qui per omnia nobis similis factus est absque peccato , non fuit ante ejus in carne adventum : qualis insaniae est, dicere alias hominum animas ante corpora esse?
passages.english: Since, moreover, Origen added this to his other blasphemies, that the soul of the Lord existed beforehand, and that God the Word was united to it before he became incarnate of the Virgin, the holy Athanasius himself, overturning this delusion too, speaks thus in the letter to Epictetus: "Rightly will all condemn themselves who think that the flesh which is from Mary existed before Mary, and that God the Word had a human soul before her, and was always in it before [his] coming." Therefore if, from what was said by the holy Athanasius, the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was made like us in all things without sin, did not exist before his coming in the flesh, what madness is it to say that the other souls of men exist before their bodies?

passages.original: At nos affirmamus, universitatis opificem corpus e terra finxisse idque animasse intelligente anima, et haec est hominis structura.» Et post alia: < Animam hominis nec ob praeterita, ut aiunt, flagitia atque scelera esse damnatam, nec in hunc demissam mundum, sapientissimus Paulus fidem facit, ita scribens: Omnes enim nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque ea quæ per corpus, prout gessit, sive bonum, sive maium (1 Cor. xv). Cur ergo propter sola propria corporis manifestari nos oportere ait, nec potius propter ea etiam quae ante corpus, si animam ante fuisse norat, et ante peccasse ? Si vero ob ea sola quae in corpore gessimus, adducimur in judicium, non utique habemus antiquius corpore peccatum : nam omnino ante id non constitit hominis anima. Hoc porro planum facit et legalis litterae vis. Si enim, ut dicit errabundus Origenes, ob snperiora commissa in supplicii ac poenae loco anima corpus accepit, quamobrem flagitiosis ac sceleratis mortem comminata est ? Magis enim oportuerat, bonos ac justos viros mortem oppetere, ut vinculis et supplicio libe- rarentur : vivere contra scelestos ac nefarios, ut poena afficerentur, nec ulla vinculorum esset liberatio.
passages.english: "But we affirm that the maker of the universe fashioned the body from earth and animated it with an intelligent soul, and this is the constitution of man." And after other things: "That the soul of man was neither condemned for past crimes and wickednesses, as they say, nor sent down into this world, the most wise Paul gives assurance, writing thus: For we must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things [done] through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (1 Cor. 15). Why then does he say that we must be made manifest only on account of the things proper to the body, and not rather also on account of things before the body, if he knew that the soul existed before and sinned before? But if we are brought into judgement only for the things we did in the body, we certainly have no sin older than the body; for the soul of man did not exist at all before it. The force of the letter of the Law also makes this plain. For if, as the wandering Origen says, the soul received the body as a place of torment and punishment for earlier offences, why did [the Law] threaten death to the wicked and criminal? For it would rather have been fitting that good and just men should meet death, so that they might be freed from bonds and punishment, and that the wicked and impious, on the contrary, should live, so that they might be punished and there might be no release from their bonds."
passages.notes: The quoted verse is 2 Cor. 5:10, though the edition cites 1 Cor. 15.

passages.original: Erat, inquit, anima ante corpus, et praeexistebat in coelis : eamque, cum ibi peccasset, in custodiam immersit Deus, id est in corpus demisit : ad purgationem, inquit, et castigationem admissorum in cœlis criminum. Hinc primum impiis- simus protinus fabulatur, veritatemque oppugnare studet. Ac paulo post: I Si ante fuit anima in coelis, ibique prius deliquit, ut malesanus Origenes Deoque repugnans dixit, non oportuit dicere sanctissimum prophetam : Et fingens spiritum hominis in ipso (Zach. XII) : sed potius, Demergens, quasi in utrem, spiritum hominis in ipso ; vel fortasse, Demittens.
passages.english: The soul, he says, existed before the body and pre-existed in the heavens; and when it had sinned there, God plunged it into custody, that is, sent it down into a body: for the purging, he says, and chastisement of crimes committed in the heavens. Here first the most impious man straightway tells fables and strives to fight against the truth. And a little later: "If the soul existed before in the heavens, and first sinned there, as the unsound Origen, who fights against God, said, the most holy prophet ought not to have said: And forming the spirit of man within him (Zech. 12), but rather: Plunging the spirit of man into him, as into a wineskin; or perhaps: Sending [it] down."

passages.original: Præterea hoc quoque Origenis demonstrat amentiam, quod affirmat coelum, et solem, et lunam, et stellas, et aquas quæ super coelos sunt, animata esse, et quasdam esse virtutes ratione utentes. Hæc vero aperte refellit sanctus Basilius in tertio sennone commentariorum in Hexaemeron, sic contra Origenis doctrinam disputans (Prope finem) : < Nobis porro de separatis aquis dicendum est et ad eos qui ab Ecclesia exciderunt, qui sub obtentu sensus anagogici et sublimiorum videlicet sententiarum, ad allegoriam confugerunt, et asserunt virtutes quasdam spirituales et incorporeas tropice ab aquis.significari ;
passages.english: Besides, this too shows Origen's madness, that he affirms that the heaven, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the waters that are above the heavens are animate, and are certain rational powers. These things the holy Basil openly refutes in the third homily of his commentaries on the Hexaemeron, arguing thus against Origen's teaching (near the end): "We must further speak about the separated waters, and against those who have fallen away from the Church, who under pretext of an anagogical sense and, forsooth, of loftier meanings, have taken refuge in allegory, and assert that certain spiritual and incorporeal powers are figuratively signified by the waters;

passages.original: xx), discipulis visus est, eisque ostendit foramina manuum ac pedum, et plagam lateris : et post resurrectionem comedit, non ut cibo indigens, sed ut eo modo resuscitati corporis naturam confirmaret. Et quidem cum Dominus ascenderet, angelos ad discipulos dixit: Hic Jesus qui assumptus est a vobis in coelum, sic veniet quemadmodum vidistis eum euntem in cælum (Act. I). Quod si, ut insanit Origenes, orbiculatum erat corpus Domini, quomodo potuit demonstrare manuum ac pe- dum foramina, aut lateris plagam? aut quomodo comedere potuit, aut omnino a discipulis agnosci? Et quoniam . modo sanctorum corpora quae post Domini resurrectionem surrexerunt (Matth.
passages.english: [20]) appeared to the disciples, and showed them the holes of his hands and feet and the wound of his side; and after the resurrection he ate, not as needing food, but so as in this way to confirm the nature of the risen body. And indeed, when the Lord ascended, the angels said to the disciples: This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven (Acts 1). But if, as Origen raves, the Lord's body was spherical, how could he show the holes of his hands and feet, or the wound of his side? Or how could he eat, or be recognised by the disciples at all? And how could the bodies of the saints which rose after the Lord's resurrection (Matt.
passages.notes: Opening fragment continues a citation (John 20) from the preceding context. "Et quoniam . modo" read as "Et quomodo".

passages.original: Qui porro Origenis impronam opinionem tuentur, firma hæc argumenta fugientes , suumque conantes tegere errorem , quaedam sanctorum Patrum dicta male excipientes, pravcque ex sententia sua interpretantes, proprio morbo accommodant: quod etiam in divinis faciunt Scripturis. Nos autem ex ipsis sanctis Patribus ostendemus inanes ac futiles eorum rationes esse. Ilaec igitur scribit sanctus Gregorius Theologus in apologetica oratione : < Nobis vero, quibus periclitatur salus animae beatae atque immortalis, quaeque sempiternam aditura est vel pœnam vel laudem , propter malitiam aut virtutem , quanti faciendum est hoc certamen, aut quanta scientia opus est?
passages.english: Those, moreover, who defend Origen's wicked opinion, fleeing these firm arguments and trying to cover their error, misconstrue certain sayings of the holy Fathers, interpret them perversely according to their own view, and adapt them to their own disease; which they also do with the divine Scriptures. But we shall show from the holy Fathers themselves that their reasonings are empty and worthless. These things, then, the holy Gregory the Theologian writes in his apologetic oration: "But for us, for whom the salvation of the blessed and immortal soul is at stake, a soul that will go to everlasting punishment or praise according to its wickedness or virtue, how highly must this contest be esteemed, or how much knowledge is needed?

passages.original: Pythagoras ergo, et Plato, et Plotinus, aliique horum sectatores, qui unico consensu animas immortales esse fatentur, eas corporibus priores affirmant, et esse quamdam animarum multitudinem, et quae delinquunt, in corpora demitti, ut dixi, et pigrorum quidem animas abire in asinos, rapacium vero in lupos, dolosorum in vulpes, mulierum amore fruentium in equos. Sed Ecclesia divinis astipulans Scripturis, animam una cum corpore creatam aflirmat, non alterum altero prius, ut vecordi Origeni visum est. Propter has igitur nefarias et perniciosas opiniones, imo potius nugas, vos hortamur, o sanctissimi Patres, It in unum collecti, subjectam expositionem diligenter perlegatis, ct singula ejus capita damnetis, et anathematizetis una cum Origene omnes qui idem sentiunt, aut senlient ad finem.
passages.english: Pythagoras, then, and Plato, and Plotinus, and the others who follow them, who with one consent confess that souls are immortal, affirm that they are prior to bodies, and that there is a certain multitude of souls, and that those which transgress are sent down into bodies, as I said; and that the souls of the lazy pass into asses, those of the rapacious into wolves, those of the deceitful into foxes, those who indulge in love of women into horses. But the Church, agreeing with the divine Scriptures, affirms that the soul was created together with the body, not one before the other, as seemed right to the senseless Origen. On account of these wicked and pernicious opinions, then, or rather trifles, we exhort you, most holy Fathers, gathered together into one, to read carefully the exposition set out below, and to condemn each of its chapters, and to anathematise, together with Origen, all who think the same or will think it to the end.
passages.notes: Stray "It" before "in unum" omitted as a scanning artefact.

passages.original: Et unitatem confitentes, conlusionem non facimus secundum Sabellium, dicentem, Trinitatem unam esse personam trinomium [trinonymum] eumdem Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum sanctum: nec dividentes proprietates, alienamus a Dei Patris substantia Filium et Spiritum sanctum, secundum Arii furorem, in tres diversas [naturas incidentes deitatem. Unus igitur Deus Pater, ex quo omnia : et unus unigenitus Filius, per quem omnia : et unus Spiritus sanctus, in quo omnia.
passages.english: And in confessing the unity, we do not make a confusion according to Sabellius, who says that the Trinity is one person with three names, the same being Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit; nor, in distinguishing the properties, do we estrange the Son and the Holy Spirit from the substance of God the Father, according to the madness of Arius, cutting the Godhead into three different natures. There is therefore one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things.
passages.notes: 'trinomium' is glossed by the edition as 'trinonymum' (three-named). The bracket before 'naturas' is an unclosed editorial mark, perhaps signalling a supplement; translated as reading.

passages.original: Et in mysterio igitur Christi facta unitionc, licet diversa intelligantur quæ unita sunt, sed non ipsa re et per partes a se invicem separantur ea, ex quibus dominus noster Jesus Christus compositus est, differentiam tamen consi- derantes et hanc significare volentes, numerum assuminus, et duas in Christo naturas esse dicimus: nec ideo unus Christus in duos christos, vel in duos filios dividitur. Et testimonium praestat nostris dictis sanctus Gregorius Theologus, scribens in primo libro ad Cledonium sic : « Si quis introdudt duos fllios, unum quidem ex Deo et Patre, secundum autem es matre, sed non unum eumdemque, ex adoptione eadat, quae promissa est credentibus recte.
passages.english: And so in the mystery of Christ too, the union having taken place, although the things united are understood as different, yet the things from which our Lord Jesus Christ is composed are not separated from one another in reality and by parts; nevertheless, considering the difference and wishing to signify it, we adopt number and say that there are two natures in Christ; nor is the one Christ therefore divided into two christs or two sons. And the holy Gregory the Theologian bears witness to our words, writing thus in the first book to Cledonius: "If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and the second from the mother, and not one and the same, let him fall from the adoption which is promised to those who believe rightly.

passages.original: ix): ita scribit: « Intelligendum hoc quidem quod dicit, creavit, de eo qui formam servi accepit. In his autem omnibus non duo dicimus, Deum separatim, et hominem separatim, unus enim erat: sed secundum intellectum, utriusque naturam existimantes. Sed et sanctus Gregorius Theologus in libro secundo de Filio, docens nos quomodo in Domino nostro Jesu Christo oportet naturas quæ in eo sunt, secundum intellectum discernere, ita scribit : « Cum naturæ intellectu distant, simul dividuntur etiam nomina, Paulum dicentem audi: Ut Deus Domini nostri Jeau Christi, Pater gloriæ (Ephes. I) : Christi quidem Deus, gloriae autem Pater. Nam etsi utrumque unum est, tamen non natura, sed conventu. > Et sanctus autem Gregorius Nyssenus [Episcopus Nyssæ] in quarto libro contra Eunomium, eadem nos docens, ita scribit: < Et ne aliquis incorruptibili naturæ crueis passionem applicaret, per alia manifestius talem emendat errorem, mediatorem ipsum Dei et hominum (1 Tim.
passages.english: 9) writes thus: "This which he says, 'created', is to be understood of him who took the form of a servant. But in all these things we do not speak of two, God separately and man separately, for he was one; but [we do so] in thought, considering the nature of each." But the holy Gregory the Theologian too, in the second book on the Son, teaching us how we must distinguish in thought the natures that are in our Lord Jesus Christ, writes thus: "When the natures are distinguished in thought, the names too are divided along with them. Hear Paul saying: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory (Eph. 1): God of Christ, but Father of glory. For even though both are one, yet [they are one] not by nature but by coming together." And the holy Gregory of Nyssa [bishop of Nyssa], too, in the fourth book against Eunomius, teaching us the same things, writes thus: "And lest anyone should apply the suffering of the cross to the incorruptible nature, he corrects such an error more clearly by other [words], [calling] him the mediator of God and men (1 Tim.
passages.notes: Opening continues a citation (Prov. 8 / Basil) from the preceding context.

passages.original: xx) : non dedit eis Spiritum sanctum , sed figuratim tantummodo insufflavit : sed et lHic autem etiam Gr.] confessionem, quam fecit Thomas cum palpasset manus et latus Domini post resurrectionem, dicens, Dominus meus et Deus meus (Ibidem), inquit non esse diclam a Thoma de Christo (nec enim dixit Theodorus Deum esse Christum), sed ad miraculum resurrectionis stupefactum Thomam glorificasse Deum, qui Christum resuscitavit: et quod pejus est, etiam in interpretatione quain in Actus apostolorum scripsit Theodorus, similem fecit Christum Platoni, et Manichæo, et Epicuro, et Marcioni, dicens quod sicut illorum unusquisque ex dogmate quod invenit, suos discipulos fecit vocari Platonicos, et Manichæos, et Epicureos, et Marcionistas, simili modo et cum Christus dogma invonisset, ex ipso Christianos vocari.
passages.english: 20): [that] he did not give them the Holy Spirit, but only breathed on them figuratively; and also [the] confession which Thomas made when he had touched the hands and side of the Lord after the resurrection, saying, 'My Lord and my God' (ibid.), he says was not said by Thomas about Christ (for Theodore did not say that Christ is God), but that Thomas, astonished at the miracle of the resurrection, glorified God, who raised Christ; and, what is worse, even in the commentary which Theodore wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, he made Christ like Plato, and Mani, and Epicurus, and Marcion, saying that just as each of them, from the doctrine he devised, caused his disciples to be called Platonists, and Manichaeans, and Epicureans, and Marcionites, in like manner also, since Christ had devised a doctrine, from him [people] are called Christians.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-reference (John 20). 'lHic autem etiam Gr.]' is an intruded editorial note (apparently 'The Greek here also [has]...') and is omitted. Scanning errors corrected: 'diclam' > 'dictam', 'quain' > 'quam', 'invonisset' > 'invenisset'.

passages.original: Ipsis enim Arianis ad decipiendos populos suo errori coujungentibus Dionysium, qui ante multos annos Athanasii [multis annis ante Athanasium] fuit Alexandriae episcopus, et dicentibus quod et ipso Dionysius similia eis sapuit, Athanasius magnus Ecclesiæ doctor multis modis ostendit in scriptis, rectam fidem Dionysium ab initio prædicasse, nulloque modo participem Arianæ impietatis fuisse. Isti autem hærctica sapientes, suam impietatem eidem synodo ap- plicare festinant. Qualis autem est condemnatio, et qualis imminet maledictio eis qui in Patres peccant, docet nos et divina Scriptura.
passages.english: For when the Arians themselves, in order to deceive the people, were linking to their own error Dionysius, who was bishop of Alexandria many years before Athanasius, and were saying that Dionysius too held views like theirs, Athanasius, the great teacher of the Church, showed in many ways in his writings that Dionysius had preached the right faith from the beginning and had in no way been a sharer in the Arian impiety. But these men, who hold heretical views, hasten to attach their own impiety to that same synod. And what kind of condemnation, and what kind of curse, hangs over those who sin against the Fathers, the divine Scripture also teaches us.
passages.notes: The text has a doublet: 'ante multos annos Athanasii [multis annis ante Athanasium]', evidently an editorial correction of the same phrase; translated once. 'coujungentibus' read as 'conjungentibus', 'ipso' as 'ipse', 'hærctica' as 'hæretica'.

passages.original: Ut autem nihil subtilitatis prætermittamus, necessarium putavimus memorare etiam illa quae ab Augusto sanctæ memoriam Africano episcopo scripta sunt. Quaestione enim aliqua post mortem Cæciliani de eo mota, quod ab ecclesiastica traditione declinasse dicebatur, et propter hoc quibusdam a catholica Ecclesia separatis, scribit ad Bonifacium idem sanctus Augustinus, quod non oportebat, aliquos ideo separare sese a catholica Ec< clesia. Si enim vera essent ea quæ Cæciliano inferebantur, et manifestatus esset contrarium aliquid ecclesiastico statui sapuisse, etiam post mortem eum anathemati subjicerem.
passages.english: But so that we may leave out nothing of precision, we have thought it necessary to recall also the things that were written by Augustine of holy memory, the African bishop. For when some question was raised after the death of Caecilian concerning him, that he was said to have departed from ecclesiastical tradition, and when on this account some had separated from the catholic Church, the same holy Augustine writes to Boniface that some ought not for that reason to separate themselves from the catholic Church. 'For if the things charged against Caecilian were true, and it had been made evident that he had held something contrary to the Church's standing, I would subject him to anathema even after death.'
passages.notes: 'Augusto' read as 'Augustino', 'memoriam' as 'memoriae'. The last sentence shifts to the first person ('subjicerem'), so it is taken as a quotation of Augustine; the shift is abrupt in the Latin. 'ecclesiastico statui' is rendered 'the Church's standing'; it may mean the Church's established order or teaching.
